PORT ABINO LIGHTHOUSE-RIGHT TO VISIT PUBLIC WORKS AND INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
I rise on a question of privilege which affects my rights as a member of this house.
While in the neighbourhood of Fort Erie on Saturday, June 10, I was taken by members of the Association for the Preservation of the Erie East Lakefront to see the federal lighthouse at Port Abino. We took the only access road, drawing up at the home of the lighthouse keeper. A neighbouring resident backed his car from the garage squarely across the road, barring our way back. An argument ensued, following which he gave us 20 minutes to get off the road before he would call the police. As we were ready to go, we left without further ado, although I may say not without reluctance on our part.
Now, here is my point of privilege. As a federal member of parliament I believe I have every right to visit public works which are paid for by the taxpayers, yet I was ordered off the access road by a local resident. He claimed that the courts had given him and other local residents the right to bar the road to the public. Yet this road is plowed in winter by the township at public expense.
Further, I was informed that in recent times the residents have moved the gate to the private section of the road so as to include about a quarter of a mile more than the court is supposed to have awarded them. This, Mr. Speaker, is a completely unwarranted interference with the rights of a member of this house to visit public works and institutions. I ask you to take steps to correct this situation without delay.

Hon. Gordon Churchill (Winnipeg South
Centre): Mr. Speaker, this is a report of a committee asking for a reduction in the quorum from 13 to eight members. The committee consists of 24 members, as is the case with most of the committees of the house and here we are, only in the 30th day of a new session, with it asking for a reduction in the quorum. This occurred apparently at the first or second meeting of the committee. I notice that three other committees earlier asked for a reduction in quorum. There is another motion on the order paper asking for a reduction. It is obvious that something has gone wrong with the committee system.
We were treated two years ago to a great move in this house toward reform, with large numbers of committees being set up. Everything was to be done, apparently, by committee procedure. The membership of most of the committees was set at a figure of 24 members, and the quorum of each committee or of most of the committees was set at a majority of the

members. At that time I recall that I pointed out the ineffectiveness of this system. I opposed the multiplicity of committees and pointed out that the quorum arrangement might be ineffective.
It is rather strange that at the opening of a new session a committee should be rushing back to this house asking for a reduction in its quorum. These committees are all miniatures of the House of Commons. The majority in the house is held by the Liberal government. The majority in each committee is held by the Liberal government. This is an obvious indication that the Liberal government is unable to man the committees.
The experience over the last year and a half, when we had the longest session in living memory, was that, with one or two exceptions the members of the opposition pretty well sustained the committees that were in operation.

I am very much opposed to this motion, sir. If we are going to have a committee system of the magnitude of that which has been imposed upon this House of Commons, then it is up to those who proposed the scheme to make it work. It was the Liberal party that proposed having all these committees that we have. It was the Liberal party that said that this is the way that parliament ought to work.
Some of us on this side, Mr. Speaker, oppose this idea. We think that this will destroy the effectiveness of the House of Commons
June 19, 1967

itself, and I think this has been proven over the last year and a half. The effectiveness and importance of the House of Commons has been reduced because of the committee work that is going on. There has to be a certain amount of committee work, of course, but a multiplicity of committees is destructive of the House of Commons. Now, at a time when this is evident, the government rushes back into the house crying for assistance, saying in effect that they cannot field a quorum and that they want the quorums reduced.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
This, sir, is obviously extremely bad. When the rules committee under the present government house leader was working last session, why did it not come up with some idea regarding the quorum of the committees which had already proved to be ineffective? No such suggestion to amend the rules was made. Now at this time of the year, in the month of June, after we have been sitting almost continuously for a year and a half, with a desire to rush to completion some of that work of the house, members on the government side come forward with the idea of reducing the quorum. This idea stems from the activity of the government house leader who wants this house to rush through in a few days our consideration of $9 billion in expenditures.
We can now see what the plan is. Quite a number of estimates have been referred to committees, these committees are to deal with them and send them back to the House of Commons with the statement that they have given them serious consideration. What are we going to find? We are going to find in connection with one committee that eight people may be given the authority to deal with the estimates of a department, and yet another committee may have nine; so eight or nine people will have the authority to discuss and deal with the estimates before the committee, and report back to the house that the estimates have been approved. We will then hear from the government side that there is no need to discuss these estimates here in the house because they have been settled in the committee. We will have about eight people in the committee carrying out the discussions, and then the house will be bemused by the suggestion of the government house leader that everything has been settled satisfactorily in the committee.
We have observed a spectacle during the last two years, and we are told that the committee work is superior to the work of the
Justice and Legal Affairs House of Commons. I suggest to you, sir, that the committee work has fallen down here in parliament, and proof of that fact is now right in front of us in this suggestion that quorums are too large, that committees are too large and should be reduced in size so everything can be speedily pushed through.
What is being made of this institution is a rubber stamp institution, to rubber stamp things in the committee, and then rubber stamp them in the house and then, through a propaganda campaign, it will be said that this is the way things ought to be done. I am here to object to this procedure, and I object to this proposed reduction of the committee quorum from 13 to eight.

Is is rather difficult for me to understand how your council could approve such a resolution without acquainting itself with the situation before reaching such a decision.
Regarding the establishment of a sanctuary for harp seals in the gulf of St. Lawrence, while this might be possible, it would only affect about 15 to 20 per cent of the seal hunt which takes place in north Atlantic waters every year. Futhermore, over 30,000 fishermen depend on the fishery resources of the gulf of St. Lawrence for a livelihood. An adult seal consumes as much as 15 pounds of fish per day, and one can judge what quantity of fish can be consumed by the seal herds when, as in 1966, lj million adult seals were spotted on the ice in the gulf of St. Lawrence alone.
I have a responsibility to protect the fishery resources of the gulf of St. Lawrence and it would be unfair to the fishermen of the Atlantic provinces if I would permit the seal herds to increase to such an extent that the fishery production of the gulf could be seriously affected.
With regard to finding alternative modes of employment for these fishermen during the months
of March and April, here again I would have hoped that your council would have been fully aware of the conditions in that part of the country during that particular period. At this time of the yeai no other means of livelihood is possible for these men. It would be very costly to the taxpayers of this country to suggest that governmental assistance be provided for the inhabitants of the St. Lawrence area who depend partly on the seal hunt at a time of the year when no other fishery operation is possible. Besides the seal hunt taking place in Zone 1 of the gulf of St. Lawrence, where sealers and aircraft are allowed to operate and where a fixed quota of 50,000 whitecoats is imposed, we also have to provide for thousands of landsmen along the coast of Newfoundland and the north shore of the St. Lawrence where seals are available only when drift ice is carried along these coasts. Mr. Speaker, in the same area but on a different subject I should like to ask the right hon. gentleman whether in view of newspaper reports that his announcement last Friday of $2.5 million of food relief to the Middle East related to aid already allocated to that area before the present difficulties arose in the Middle East and that only the $20,000 for medical supplies which the right hon. gentleman announced was additional aid, would he be good enough to clarify the situation as to Canadian aid to the Middle East and also inform the house whether the government is giving serious consideration to increasing the aid both for those needing medical attention
June 19, 1967

Inquiries of the Ministry and for the hundreds of thousands of Arabs and others needing assistance urgently at the present time?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-CANADIAN AID IN DISTRIBUTION OF SUPPLIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the existing emergency we are very fortunate in having appropriations for aid to the Middle East area already voted by parliament to the extent of $2.5 million, $1 million for UNRWA and $1 million under the food program to the Middle East. These appropriations have been voted and they are available now for food relief to that area. What the government is anxious to do now is to expedite shipments under that program under these appropriations, but that, of course, is not enough and it may be that additional appropriations will be required or additional expenditures made, which I hope can later be approved by appropriations for emergency purposes. I mentioned one of these the other day, a $20,000 grant to the Red Cross for medical supplies. We as the government have been anxious to find out from the international Red Cross and from UNRWA what they need as emergency supplies at this moment. Over the week end we have learned that what they need now is a means of rapid distribution and communications. They have sufficient supplies in the area as a whole for short term needs but they need means of distribution. They also want to be reassured that the pipe lines will be filled as they use them up for emergency purposes.
The government has agreed to help in both these respects. We are purchasing and making available to UNRWA a de Havilland Beaver aircraft for which they specifically asked for communication purposes. We have also offered to make available to UNRWA at once an airlift for long range transport which would help them in the distribution of supplies. Indeed we could make that airlift available if they so require, for the provision of long range food supplies from Canada. However, at the moment they have emphasized they have enough supplies of food, but they want to keep the pipe lines filled. Our additional assistance of a Beaver aircraft and long range aircraft transport, if they require it, would require a special appropriation which we will be bringing forward before long if we need to do these things.

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-CANADIAN AID IN DISTRIBUTION OF SUPPLIES
speechtext:
I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I am grateful to the right hon. gentleman for his answer and for the additional assistance he has announced. Would he be good enough to inform the house whether when UNRWA says it has enough

supplies for immediate needs they are referring only to those who were formerly in the refugee camps or were referring also to additional displaced persons who unfortunately and unavoidably have appeared in various areas?

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-CANADIAN AID IN DISTRIBUTION OF SUPPLIES
speechtext: In our communications with UNRWA through our embassies abroad, both in Geneva and in Beirut, we have learned that UNRWA is taking into consideration the additional refugees' requirements, but they are not yet sure of the scope of these additional requirements and as soon as we get additional information-and other governments would be getting it also-we will know whether they will require additional food relief for the additional refugees, which we will be able to help supply. However, at the moment they have enough for their needs as they can ascertain them at the moment.

speechtext:
Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin (Minister of Energy,
Mines and Resources) moved the second reading of Bill No. C-135, to establish the Cape Breton Development Corporation.
He said:

Mr. Speaker, I indicated at the resolution stage the historical, economic and social background of this question of Cape Breton coal. I also indicated the schedule of events that led to the present legislation. I have motivated the federal intervention by showing the economic and social seriousness of the problem, concluding that it was in the national interest to such a point that it went beyond the limits of Cape Breton and the financial and economic capacity of the province of Nova Scotia.
I have also mentioned the fine co-operation received from the provincial government and my colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen), insisted on this point.
I have summarized the agreement reached by the Canadian government and the government of Nova Scotia. This agreement gave a pretty good idea of the contents of the bill. I will have in the course of the discussion today the opportunity to reply to various questions put last week, but I am told that I would be stretching parliamentary procedure and that I could be called to order if I were to do so now.
At the present stage, all that I can do is to introduce the legislation, that is Bill No. C-135.
The hon. members now have the bill on hand.
June 19, 1967
COMMONS DEBATES	1659

Hon. members will note that this bill has a preamble which is lor the specific purpose of establishing that the Cape Breton coal problem is of national concern. The federal government is not now in the business of closing mines when they have come to the end of their reserves; we are taking part in this particular operation it is because the Cape Breton problem is one of national importance.
The preamble also points to a relationship which exists between the phasing in of new industry and the phasing out of the coal mines. That principle is to be found elsewhere in the bill and it is a major foundation of the legislation.
Later in the bill we have clauses concerning the establishment of the corporation itself with the two divisions, the coal division and the economic industrial development division. The purpose is to assign a particular function to each division. We thought this would be a more effective way of proceeding than by having only one division within the corporation.
Farther on there are clauses concerning the acquisition of property. Hon. members who questioned me on this last week will find answers to some of their questions in these clauses. What should be acquired is specifically indicated. How it should be acquired is also indicated; three possible methods are mentioned. One is straight negotiation, one is agreed arbitration, and one is expropriation.
Hon. members who have read the bill will have already observed that the method in respect of expropriation is explained at quite some length. The reason is that the federal government is not entitled by law to acquire more than land. Therefore the expropriation procedures for the companies assets have to be spelled out.
Last week hon. members expressed concern about the pension and retirement plans for miners. The answer to their questions is to be found in clause 18. The pension plan concerns those who are now employed, those who have been employed, and those who will be employed by the company or corporation as the case may be. Members will also observe that the corporation is instructed to establish an early retirement program.
The objectives and powers of the coal division are also clearly indicated. There is an interesting proviso covering the presentation by the coal division of an over-all plan within one year of the coming into force of the legislation. Members may think that this is
Cape Breton Development Corporation demanding too much too quickly of the corporation. Consequently there are other clauses dealing with possible amendments of that plan. In a way this is the same thing as we did with the Expo '67 corporation. Hon. members will recall that that corporation presented a plan within months after the passage of the legislation establishing it and that the plan was later amended and improved upon.
There are also a number of clauses dealing with the functions and powers of the industrial development division. Those of us who have read the bill have observed that these functions and powers are very wide. We have, of course, kept maximum flexibility. The corporation will be on the spot, as it were, and able to devise what is best in the interest of the people of Cape Breton.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
At the same time, Mr. Speaker, we are trying to avoid duplication. There will be a committee of officials to co-ordinate the actions of all departments, federal and provincial alike, in order to achieve maximum efficiency. We also have financial provisions both on the coal production side and on the economic development side. I am sure that in these provisions members have found answers to some of the questions they were asking me in connection with what the $25 million was for, and so on. However, if members are not sufficiently clear we can go back to these explanations during the clause by clause study.
To conclude the bill, Mr. Speaker, there are clauses of general interest. For example, there is a clause providing that the head office of the corporation will be at Sydney so that members of the corporation will as much as possible be au fait with developments there. There is also provision made for winding up the corporation. The corporation is being set up to achieve a certain job of work which will take a certain number of years. We hope that success on the industrial development side will make it possible for the corporation to wind up at the end of the anticipated 15 years or even less.
There is also an interesting clause at the end of the bill which establishes the constitutional basis for federal action. This clause refers to works and undertakings declared to be for the general advantage of Canada.
There it is, Mr. Speaker. I have tried to give a bird's-eye view of the bill. So we have before us then, a bill which arises out of an agreement between Canada and Nova Scotia to establish, the Cape Breton Development Corporation, to modernize and operate the
June 19. 1967

Cape Breton Development Corporation coal mines, and also to effect in an enlightened manner the transfer of the economy of Cape Breton Island from coal production to other forms of industrial development and economic activity.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OVER COAL UNDERTAKINGS, DEVELOPING INDUSTRY, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope I will be as brief in what I have to say as the minister in order to facilitate the passing of this legislation. I admit that the bill is very much in line with previous policy statements and with the policy announced on October 5, 1965 by the then minister of labour at Halifax.
The answers to the questions which were asked and which no doubt will be asked when we go through the bill clause by clause will clarify many points. However, I would ask the minister to prepare himself to explain some remarks which were made in this chamber on Thursday when we were dealing with the resolution. Among those remarks I would ask him to give a complete explanation of what was meant by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) when he said as reported at page 1579 of Hansard:
-in the meantime build up alternative industries so that there wil be a cushioning effect on displacement and so that the total economy and the total community will be protected.
The word "protected" is the key word. The purpose of the original policy statement and the intent of the legislation were to assure the miners of Cape Breton that there would be no displacements until alternative work was provided. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, you can readily understand why the minister said that we have to give consideration to the cushioning effect. I would ask the minister when he deals with this question to assure the house that alternative employment will be made available before any miner is displaced.
Let me point out once again that this will be a fairly tricky task to bring about. As I indicated on Thursday, you cannot close out a mine by displacing miners one, two, five or ten at a time. A substantial work force would have to be displaced at one time in order to bring about an orderly closing of any coal mine.
If I may now review the bill and at the same time tie in the statements made by the minister a moment ago, I am of the conviction that coal mining will continue in Cape Breton for a long time to come. The phasing-out period of 15 years that is being legislated for would not necessarily bring about the closure of any colliery; at least, I hope this will not be the case. In this regard I refer to

the fact that the sum of $25 million is to be expended on the improvement of mechanization. This should go a long way toward solving the problems faced by the mines at the moment.
In this regard I would impress upon all members of the house the importance of getting this legislation through so that collieries such as No. 20 in Glace Bay and No 12 in New Waterford will be given some financial assistance in order to proceed with modernization as quickly as possible. The same comment applies to No. 26 colliery, which last year hoisted over one million tons of coal despite the fact that it was using obsolete equipment. With this capital expenditure on modernization of equipment in coal mines, it is possible that the remaining collieries will have a long life ahead of them.
May I now deal with a statement made by the minister a moment ago. He referred to the end of the resources in this area. I hope that in referring to the end of the resources he made a comparison between the estimate of coal reserves in Cape Breton by Dr. Donald and that made by Mr. Justice Rand. Apparently they are a long way apart.
As for the bill itself and the acquisition of the Dominion Coal Company interest, I am somewhat concerned about certain recent statements. I understand that very recently in London Sir Roy Dobson informed his shareholders that the assets of the Dominion Coal Company were worth $53 million. I hope the government is not going to use this figure as a yardstick because not too long ago this same company considered its assets to be nothing more nor less than worthless, at least worthless from the point of view of putting them on the market for sale. No private interest or anybody else would have touched them. I hope the government will give serious consideration to the amount to be paid to the company for these assets.
I also hope it will take into consideration the argument I put forward during the resolution stage to the effect that any exchange of funds between the government and the Dominion Coal Company should have the rider attached that this money will be left in Cape Breton to develop whatever industries the people there care to carry on. At the moment I can think of nothing but the further development of the mines, though the money could perhaps be used to better advantage in Sydney in order to diversify the operations of the steel plant. While speaking of the diversification of the operations of the Sydney steel plant, may I
June 19, 1967

say that I trust that in negotiating any business deal with Dosco in the near future, the government, in order to alleviate concern in the Sydney area, will get from Dosco a firm commitment in respect of its plans for the Sydney steel operations.
I realize that this bill is tied in exclusively with the coal question, and in this regard I would ask the minister to note a few questions I should like to ask so that while we are dealing with the bill clause by clause he can provide answers thereto. I should like to ask him about clause 2 and its reference to the Sydney and Louisburg Railway Company. It is my understanding that this company went out of existence when it was amalgamated with the Cumberland Railway Company. If there is something to be dealt with in respect of the Sydney and Louisburg Railway Company I hope the minister will inform the house.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
I should also like to ask the minister to tell us what the situation is in respect of the railway line between Broughton and Louisburg. Why does the bill not provide for taking over this line? That would be natural if the corporation is to take over the assets of the Cumberland Railway Company and the Sydney and Louisburg Railway. What is the intention in this regard if there is no rolling stock or anything else involved? What is the reason for not taking over that section?
It is also of interest to note that there is nothing mentioned about the salaries, fees and expenses of the president, the chairman and members of the board. Perhaps this is not of great importance, but the minister could possibly give an explanation in this regard.
Clause 9 (b) makes reference to the acquisition of all interests of the companies in lands and all personal property located under the waters adjacent to the county of Cape Breton, and later makes further reference to these interests of the companies. I should like the minister to explain this situation. At this time we are waiting for the decision of the supreme court in reference to the ownership of offshore mineral rights. Since this question is before the supreme court, what does this reference mean? How can this bill be interpreted in light of that situation? Does it mean that the federal government is purchasing something to which it has already laid claim in the courts of this land? Perhaps I am misconstruing the whole approach, but in reading the bill it seems that all the interests in the lands under the waters adjacent to Cape Breton are to be purchased from the 27053-106
Cape Breton Development Corporation Dominion Coal Company. Does the government have prior knowledge as to the decision which will be handed down by the supreme court? If not, why is such a move being made, the result of which will be that the government will buy from the Dominion Coal Company something it now claims it owns?
As I indicated, Mr. Speaker, I intend to be as brief as possible so that the very necessary improvements which will follow the adoption of this bill can be commenced as quickly as possible at the collieries I mentioned, namely, Nos. 12, 20 and 26 which are within my riding. Of course, the hon. members for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. Muir) and for Pictou (Mr. MacEwan), will have something to say in respect of the colleries in their areas.
As a result of the establishment of this corporation there will have to be some deviation from a policy announced earlier by the minister to which I took objection. He announced a fixed subvention policy for a five year period. I assume that this policy will have to be changed or eliminated because of the obvious intention of this bill. Perhaps the minister could also make clear to the house the financial status of the Dominion Coal Company in respect of what is owed to the federal government because of loans or other advances. There is a reference in the bill to what is owed to Her Majesty by the Dominion Coal Company.
I will defer any further questions I may have until we reach the clause by clause examination of the bill. I hope the bill will receive speedy passage by the house.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OVER COAL UNDERTAKINGS, DEVELOPING INDUSTRY, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I said last Thursday during the resolution stage, I wish it were possible to accept this very important piece of legislation without being forced to criticize some of its basic aspects. When the Donald report came down-I do not have it before me-and when the present legislation was forecast in government announcements, it was made clear that the government was not prepared to accept Dr. Donald's timetable for phasing out coal operations. I am not quoting, but I think I can paraphrase the announcement accurately. The government was determined to gear the phasing out of the coal operations to the development of new job opportunities for those persons who might be affected. I suggest that somewhere during the drafting of this legislation that basic undertaking was lost and seriously departed from. As a result a great number of questions arise in my mind
June 19, 1967
1662	COMMONS
Cape Breton Development Corporation and in the mind of anyone who studies this bill carefully.
First of all, I find that the corporation is required by law to provide the minister, and through him the governor in council with an over-all plan within one year from the enactment of this legislation. That over-all plan must have in it not only items relating to the conduct of coal mining and related operations by the corporation but also a blueprint for the progressive reduction of coal production by the corporation and the discontinuance of coal production by mines that are not economically viable.
Let me ask the minister how it can conceivably be possible for the corporation to present the government with a plan for phasing out coal production within one year of its establishment and take into account possible new jobs for displaced miners? How is it conceivable that the corporation can do that? Because it is not conceivable I suggest that is why the legislation contains clause 17(4) which deals with the considerations that the corporation has to keep in mind before eliminating or substantially reducing the production of coal.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
One consideration it must bear in mind is that such closing down or substantially reducing the production of coal must be within the plan or the amended plan-I am paraphrasing the clause-and the other is that it should take all reasonable measures to reduce as far as possible any unemployment or economic hardship that can be expected to result therefrom. It was my understanding from reading the government pronouncement that after accepting the general principle of dealing with the problem by a crown corporation the government was determined, as it should have been, that there would not be any phasing out of the coal operation until such time as alternative jobs were in fact available.
I say to the minister and to government that they are going to compound the problems of Cape Breton Island and cause increasing hardship for the people of that island if the principles involved in the clause giving the power to reduce coal production, and in the clause requiring the corporation to reduce as far as possible any unemployment resulting therefrom, remain unchanged. I am not suggesting that it is wise for Cape Breton or for Canada to continue operating an industry if it is proven to be an industry which ought not to be operated. I am not at all convinced that this is the case with regard to the entire coal industry or that it is the case with regard to
[Mr. Lewis.)

the coal industry in Cape Breton Island. But I am not going to pose as an expert. That is a decision which I am quite prepared to leave to the corporation that will be established.
But it is totally wrong in principle, and does not deal with the problems of Cape Breton Island, to give the corporation the authority to throw miners out of work before alternative jobs are available. This is precisely what this bill does. This is absolutely contrary to the undertaking which the government gave, if I understood its undertaking. This legislation ought to read as clearly as words can make it that the corporation shall not cause any unemployment among the miners until such time as it is satisfied that the other division of the corporation, the industrial development division, has progressed sufficiently to guarantee alternative employment for the miners thus displaced.
It is not sufficient for the minister to point, as he may well do, to the provision in clause 18 (2) with respect to what I suppose may be called lump sum severance pay for miners who become unemployed or are retired early as a result of the reorganization by the corporation of the coal mining industry. I hope the minister believes the statements I am making to be sincere, as I believe every statement he has made to be sincere. I did not have to make this kind of criticism, because I recognize the importance of this legislation. But I say that when the corporation is asked all through this bill to rehabilitate and organize the coal industry so that it will produce "efficiently", which in commercial terms means profitably or at least with as little loss as possible-let me put it that way as in his case it is probably more accurate-the coporation may easily throw hundreds of miners out on the streets before there is alternative employment. Paying them lump sum severance pay will not do anything for them. If they are men of 40, 45 or over, as most of them will probably be because of the age situation among coal miners, giving them a small lump sum-it would have to be small; it cannot be very large-by way of severance pay will not save their lives. They may well not be able to do the kind of thing that is necessary in order to move elsewhere where there may be jobs.
I see no reason for this provision, and I emphasize, underline and repeat this because it seems to me to go to the core of the problem. In my respectful submission the core of the problem is that no coal miner on Cape Breton Island should lose one day's work as a result of the reorganization by the
June 19, 1967

corporation of the coal industry. Not a single coal miner should be laid off by the corporation until the other arm has created jobs to which those miners may go. Not until then should the closing down of mines or the reduction of coal production take place.
I am very seriously concerned about the general powers given the corporation in clause 17(1) of the bill and the obvious intention that there be unemployment among the miners for a period provided in the last part of clause 17. As I said, this seems to me to be entirely contrary to the definite commitment made by the government that unemployment would not take place and that the reduction in coal production would be geared to the provision of new and alternative jobs for those who may be displaced by such reduction.
I had hoped that the point I have just raised would not have to be made, but I was really shocked, if I may put it that way, by these provisions when I read them for the first time this morning. When we are in committee I hope amendments will be put forward to these clauses. I invite my hon. friends, and I am sure they are friends, of the official opposition who share this view to put forward amendments in this respect. I will be glad to support any amendment they propose to these clauses. If they do not introduce any, I will try to bring forward amendments that will take from the corporation the power to cause unemployment among the coal miners without the provision of alternative jobs.
The second point that concerns me, as it concerned me on Thursday last, is the provision for compensation to Dosco. I shall not belabour the point. I say again that on any basis of equity, morality and social justice the preferred shareholders of this corporation are not entitled to be paid for being relieved of a financial liability, and they are certainly not entitled to be paid out of the public treasury. I regret that the government has seen fit to make provision in the bill for such payment. But I regret something else even more, and that is the abdication by the government of its responsibility in this field.
It is not the responsibility of the corporation to be established to negotiate with the company regarding compensation. That is a direct responsibility of government. Government has to make that decision. Apparently negotiations have taken place and have got nowhere. I judge this to be so because in answer to questions asked by various hon. members we were informed that talks were 27053-1065
Cape Breton Development Corporation proceeding with the company with regard to this program. Apparently these talks have not reached a conclusion. I appreciate fully that the corporation, if I remember correctly, has to receive the approval of the governor in council before it can actually agree to any particular compensation, but that is not good enough. Surely the right way to do this is for the government, with all the power that the government has and with all the responsibility which it carries with regard to the people of Cape Breton, to the taxpayers of Canada and to everyone else, to negotiate the takeover. Of course it would be, but it would be a responsibility that it could carry out just as effectively and just as competently as the responsibility to modernize and operate the coal mines. Will it be based on the value of the salvage that can be obtained from the mining operations? That would be one basis for settling the amount of compensation, and that is provided for in clause 9. Mr. Chairman, I think I should first try to answer some of the rather general questions asked. Perhaps I could leave the more specific questions for the clause by clause study of the bill. The hon. member for York South has already remedied some of the rather disagreeable things that were said the other night on the subject of subventions. If I referred so extensively to subventions, call them what you will, the $200 million spent in the past, the $31 million spent last-year and the $27 million that could be spent next year, there was certainly no attempt on my part to shame the miners. I was simply trying to underline the fact that all this money could be used to better avail. I was trying to convince my colleagues of the necessity to move as fast as we can in broadening the economic base of Cape Breton.
I point this out, Mr. Chairman, because the other night I had the feeling that I was being pushed on the side of the big power corporations in this country. The hon. member for Longueuil is the son of a mailman, the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond is the son of a miner, and I am the son of a railroad man. I do not have the feeling of representing the big corporations of this country. This was rather implied in the debate and I did not particularly like it.
The second point with which I should like to deal concerns the inclusion of steel in the
1672	COMMONS
Cape Breton Development Corporation present legislation. Several hon. members have raised the point that we should add steel to coal under this legislation. Neither I nor the Liberal party are opposed to nationalization in principle or practice, because that is exactly what we are now doing. But I think one must not abuse nationalization. I believe this is the way the majority of the population feels. If we were to take over Cape Breton steel production today there are many other fields of mining in Canada, gold mines, for example, that might claim a similar advantage. Other areas of the Canadian economy which are subsidized might request similar treatment. As a general theory I believe that nationalization should be brought about very sparingly indeed.
My own opposition to the proposal that steel be included in the legislation is certainly not a theoretical one. I simply feel that this development corporation will be busy enough dealing with the subject of coal that it should not also become involved in steel. But of course everybody recognizes that indirectly the development corporation will contribute by its success in the industrial development field to the improvement of the economic situation in the island, and consequently indirectly to the situation in the steel industry. If I believe the newspapers, this is the way the premier of Nova Scotia feels; if I can believe my own ears, this is also the way the coal miners of Cape Breton feel, namely, that this corporation should be directly involved in their operations even if indirectly it can have an influence upon the whole of the economic situation in Cape Breton.
My third main point concerns the phasing in, phasing out question. The hon. member for York South seemed to be saying that there is nothing in the bill on that subject though he realizes it was in the Prime Minister's declaration of December last. I was rather surprised to hear the hon. member quoting at length from clause 17 and not mentioning the end of clause 17 (1). This clause deals with the plan. It is said very specifically at the end of clause 17 (1) that the plan shall take into account progress in providing employment outside the coal producing industry and in broadening the base of the economy of Cape Breton Island. I think the relationship between the phasing in of industry and the phasing out of coal mining is very clearly stated in that clause. You find the same idea in the preamble to the bill at the bottom of page 1:
-and the progressive withdrawal oi the corporation from such production in accordance with a

plan that takes into account progress in providing employment outside the coal producing industry and in broadening the base of the island's economy;
It seems to me that this relation is quite clearly indicated in the legislation. It certainly corresponds with previous commitments by the government and with what I and other ministers have in mind. So there is a relationship between phasing in and phasing out. It is a relationship only There is no doubt, in view of what the hon. member for Cape Breton South has been telling us, with which I entirely agree that it is very difficult or even impossible to phase out one mine because it becomes totally unproductive. So the phasing in, phasing out program will be in blocks of people. That is the way I see it.
With regard to the argument put forward by the hon. member for York South, it might not be possible to make sure that "no coal miner will lose one day's work." I think he was overenthusiastic and perhaps he was overdoing it when he said that, because it is quite possible that some miners will lose a few days work in the process. The important point is that they should not be hurt in the process. That can be taken care of by other methods, and I am quite sure my hon. friend would agree with me on that.

I think I could not live another five minutes without answering the hon. member for Pictou concerning the future of the McBean mine. I confess immediately that no final decision has been taken with regard to it. However, I should like to make a few comments.
The first point is that the mine is not located in the Sydney coal field defined by the present bill. It is not in an area described as "an area of national concern". Pictou county apparently is not by far in as bad shape as is Cape Breton or the Sydney-Glace Bay area in particular.
I am sure my hon. friend would agree with me that there would be a danger of establishing a dangerous precedent if the McBean mine were covered under this legislation because other mines in Canada as well as other mines in Nova Scotia have been, are being, or will be closed. It should be evident to everyone there is a danger that in similar situations people might be knocking at our door asking us to help them close their mines. May I repeat that the aim of this legislation is not to close mining operations in Canada but to protect communities which are in danger as a result of a rather general downward economic movement. So I think my hon. friend, who knows his area is developing economically, would not want to say that the McBean mine is in exactly the same position as are the other mines in eastern Cape Breton.

The second factor to bear in mind is that McBean has nearly exhausted its coal reserves. The company informs us that the mine will have to closed by December, 1968. It will have to be closed at that time if it is not closed soon and, as we have been reminded by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, one cannot phase out a single mine, it has to be done in one step. This is a very important fact. The mine has only a year and a half to two years of life, economically speaking.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
My third point, which I think is a very important one too, is that we have made an offer to the company to continue the subventions at the present level. The company implies that this is equivalent to asking them to close the mine because they cannot live on the present level of subsidy. They need an extra $3 a ton to keep it going. To keep the mine going for another year and a half or two years then means that we must spend $1.5 million, $2 million or $2.5 million, and I submit in all honesty that there might be better ways of using this money than simply to prolong the life of the mine. We must bear in mind that the operation must be performed in a year or two. The operation must be performed sooner or later. It is traumatic, sad -you can use any word you care to use- but it must be performed. We have no choice. It is not a matter of should we or should we not bring this mine to a close; it must be closed for lack of reserves.
As the hon. member for Pictou mentioned, a private operator may wish to take over the mine and continue operating it for a certain time. Even if the corporation does not take over the McBean mine-and I shall come back to this later-clause 16(d), in particular, gives the corporation authority to help. I shall do my very best to help in this process and I assure the hon. member for Pictou that I do not intend simply to look at the matter and let it slide by. If the closing of the mine is decided on now, or in three months or five months-I do not know exactly when it will be-we shall bring in all possible federal and provincial support to soften the blow. Perhaps the $2 million that will be saved might go toward helping the McBean mine. On the other hand, if we are to spend $2 million and then perform the operation I have spoken of in one and a half or two years, my case will be much weaker for wishing to do something special for the McBean mine. Again, we shall do everything to help that we can legally.

With respect to the distribution of the $2 million worth of equipment purchased by the Dominion Coal Board, as I have already written to my hon. friend, the decision is left to the company. I am told that in the McBean mine geogological irregularities have restricted the application of mechanical operating methods. There is no automatic coal cutting at McBean, and the equipment is mainly of that sort.
With respect to the hon. member's reference to Trenton, when he said that the power station was using McBean coal and that it would go on needing that coal he was quite correct. Trenton will need coal even after 1968 when the mine will be closed. I can understand his plea, but the fact that Trenton will sooner or later have to develop new sources of coal should also be borne in mind.
With respect to the Atlantic Provinces Power Development Act, as has been said, the authority for the power subsidy continues to November, 1969, and we have no intention at the moment of bringing it to a premature end. I am not in a position to say what will happen to that legislation in the future.
I have tried in my remarks to bear in mind the words of the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria, and I hope I have smiled enough during my presentation for hon. members, who have been so willing up to now to expedite the passage of this bill through the normal processes, to continue in that spirit.

speechtext:
I rise to make only two points. The minister in his answers to comments drew the attention of the committee, and my attention in particular, to the last lines of clause 17(1) which provide that plans being prepared by the corporation have to take into account progress in providing employment outside the coal producing industry, and so on. I have those words underlined; I knew they were there. But with great respect to the minister, they are irrelevant to the point I made. Indeed, they are irrelevant in terms of the statement the minister himself made some minutes ago.
The minister said, if I understood him correctly, that it was impossible for him to foretell the rhythm of the phasing in or the phasing out. He pointed to the fact that if there were only two new major industries there would be much greater difficulty than if there were five. That is my point precisely. Clause 17(1) deals with the over-all plan which the corporation has to prepare within not more than a year. I suggest that it is impossible for the corporation, just as it is impossible for the minister, to foretell the precise rhythm of development and be able to take into account progress in providing alternative employment in the future in a way which will guarantee that the two operations mesh properly. This is why I did not refer to those words in 17(1). I do not think they have any bearing on the question.
What concerns me is that clause 17(4)(b) assumes there will be unemployment and economic hardship as a result of the work of the corporation in the coal mining area. I do not think this legislation should contain such an assumption. It will be bad enough if we do
June 19, 1967

Cape Breton Development Corporation not assume it in the legislation. Let us not give the corporation the green light to take action which might result in such consequences. Some unemployment may be inevitable, as the minister has pointed out. If a decision is taken to close down a mine which employs 500 people or 1,000 people, there may well be some for whom alternative jobs cannot be obtained. But that is not what the clause says.
I may have something else to say about this clause when we get to it. I merely wish to say respectfully to the minister at this point, that I was not unaware of the words in subclause (1) of clause 17, and I suggest to him that those words do not attach to the subject which concerns me at all.
We on this side of the house have drawn attention to the difficulties in the steel industry and to the urgent need to take this situation into account in the legislation before us. The minister threw up his hands almost and said-I am paraphrasing his words-that he would have felt a great deal more hopeful about the situation, indeed, he would have been ready to use superlative adjectives about it, were it not for very recent experiences. One of the recent experiences to which he referred was the number of lay-offs in the steel plant at Sydney. These lay-offs have been going on progressively throughout the last couple of months with the result that 1,100 or 1,200 steel workers are unemployed and walking the streets of Sydney as of now.
What is the minister playing with? In answer to the hon. member for Pictou who was concerned about the McBean mine the hon. gentleman very characteristically-I hope he will not think I am unkind in choosing that word-said the situation in Pictou was not quite as bad as it is in Cape Breton and therefore was not of such national concern. How bad is bad, Mr. Chairman? Does an industry have to lie flat on its back before the government and the minister will take an initiative to foresee the future and do something about it?
What are these comparisons of degrees of badness? The steel industry of Cape Breton is in bad shape now. Not only is it in bad shape, but it is perfectly obvious from reading the reports that there is a deliberate company policy at least to reduce the operation of the steel plant at Sydney and, I personally suspect, to do away with it altogether in the years to come by moving basic steel production to the Contrecoeur complex now under construction. From the point of view of Dosco there may well be good economic and finan-
cial reasons for doing so, but from the point of view of the city of Sydney and the people of Cape Breton island what is taking place there is almost as disastrous as what has been taking place in the coal industry. There is an important exception. While in the coal industry there are factors which the government cannot correct-the price of coal, the quality of the coal in certain of the seams and so on-in the steel industry these considerations do not apply. I venture to say to the minister and to the government, without much fear of contradiction, that a properly organized and diversified steel plant at Sydney could be made economically feasible if there are people who want to put in the necessary capital and produce the kind of steel products which can be used in the Atlantic provinces and in export particularly to the newer nations of the world.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I, and I am sure other members of the committee, want to know what principles there are which prevent the government from adding a provision to this legislation giving the corporation or a division of the corporation or another corporation-I do not care which-the authority to take over the Dosco steel plant or to buy out a part of it-again I do not care which-as other democratic governments have done in similar situations. Possibly the government could acquire a 51 per cent interest in the plant. I do not know the capitalization arrangements of Dosco and I am not presuming to set out a price at this time. However, it should be possible to take over the plant or gain a controlling interest in it and then set out deliberately to modernize and diversify the production of steel therein. The two are directly connected, Mr. Chairman.
If the hon. member for Cape Breton South will forgive me for interpreting and taking his question one step further-he can correct me if I am wrong-I believe he had precisely this in mind when he asked a question a moment ago with regard to a guarantee that when a miner loses his job as a result of this new arrangement another job will be made available for him. The hon. member knows as well as I do, and as well as I am sure the minister does, that if new industry is created now on Cape Breton Island there are enough unemployed presently walking the streets to fill the jobs. There are now hundreds of unemployed walking the streets of Sydney and Glace Bay. It will take some years before enough industry can be established to place these unemployed people in productive work,
June 19, 1967

not to mention making jobs available for miners and other employees who may be displaced by the operations of the corporation outlined in this bill.
Unless the minister and the government are manacled by doctrinaire prejudice about touching any private corporation except if such corporation is completely incapable of making any progress, when, if not now, should the government act on behalf of the steel plant at Sydney which is half, if not wholly, on its back? Based on the facts as they have unfurled in the past year or so, I urge the government to reconsider its position respecting the Sydney plant and indeed other steel operations in Nova Scotia. The steel industry ought to be included in this legislation.
While I am on my feet I want to say on behalf of my colleagues and myself that the hon. member for Pictou is entirely justified in insisting that the mine in his riding, Acadia Coal, a mine owned by a Dosco subsidiary, should also be brought within the terms of this legislation. What is this fear that members of the government have? Why is there this hesitation about doing a whole job, whether in the area of coal or in the area of including steel in this legislation? I appreciate that to deal with the steel plant in Sydney would be a different kind of proposition. It will undoubtedly deserve compensation that may run into many tens of millions of dollars because of equipment and facilities which are there. This is a problem the answer to which will have to be found. The company could either be bought for cash or securities could be given to the shareholders, whatever method may be found to be wisest.
The steel plant is still to some extent a going concern, but just because there may be greater complications in acquiring it is no reason for the government to sit back and let the situation go from bad to worse in the days ahead, which would present the danger of nullifying the positive steps outlined in this legislation. The progressive reduction in operations by the steel plant, in turn creating unemployment, will add to the problems with which the development section of the new corporation will have to deal.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the explanation given by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources regarding the McBean mine, but I cannot agree with him. If the minister does not know this I will tell him now that the area of Pictou has for many years existed almost entirely on coal mining. Through provincial and federal efforts the
Cape Breton Development Corporation area is now coming alive and we can see the light. The minister has said that no decision has been made on the McBean mine which employs 400 men who could be thrown out of work in short order. If I understood the minister correctly, he said that the company believes additional subventions should be paid in order to keep the mine running until 1968. He said the amount required would be about $2 million. This is money which could be well spent if the government does not amend this bill to cover that mine. But I believe the legislation should be amended to include it.
Clause 17(4) states:
Before closing or substantially reducing the production of coal from any coal mine operated by it, the corporation shall ensure that
(a)	such closing or substantial reduction in production is in accordance with and at a time provided for in the over-all plan or any modification thereof-
And more importantly:
(b)	all reasonable measures have been adopted by the corporation, either alone or in conjunction with the government of Canada or of Nova Scotia or any agency of either of such governments, to reduce as far as possible any unemployment or economic hardship that can be expected to result therefrom.
If the bill is not to be amended, then whether it costs $2 million or more I believe this mine should be carried on long enough to ensure, so far as its 400 employees are concerned, that someone else will take it over and run it, a new mine will be developed to employ part of the work force, or guarantees of other employment will be given. If this mine came under this legislation it would fall into the over-all plan for the various mines in Cape Breton. God bless them. I hope this legislation will be the salvation of the workers of that area.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
This mine in my constituency should not be phased out within a matter of months. The men should be given the opportunity of employment in another mine or guaranteed alternative employment. The mine should be carried on for more than a few months. It should be carried on at least to the end of 1968. I cannot agree with the minister in this regard and I had to put these remarks on the record. We have seen the light in Pictou county. If this mine is closed at an early date I am afraid we will be dragged back a long way economically.

subtopic: SUGGESTED PROVISION OF ADMINISTRATIVE ASSISTANTS TO MEMBERS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of providing members of parliament with administrative assistants to aid members in carrying out their responsibilities effectively through helping in such areas of activity as research and communications with officials.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this centennial year is certainly a time for assessment, for taking
[The Chairman.]
stock of the effectiveness of our national institutions, for examining them in the light of possible need for changes and improvements to help these institutions work better in the interests of our country as we move into our second century.
While there are many differences of opinion as to the areas in which change is needed and the exact nature of changes that may be dictated by circumstances, there certainly appears to be a consensus about one extremely vital area-the need for reform and improvement of parliament. This consensus appears to exist both in parliament itself and, I think, on the part of the majority of the Canadian people.

maintopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED

speechtext: What is your evidence for that?

maintopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
subtopic: SUGGESTED PROVISION OF ADMINISTRATIVE ASSISTANTS TO MEMBERS
speechtext:
The federal government is a vast apparatus with some 300,000 employees, if we include the crown corporations, handling in this coming fiscal year a budget of close to $11 billion.
I think the public expects its elected representatives to be in a position to oversee effectively the working of this apparatus, to be aware of the directions it is taking, to decide what these directions should be in the future and to make sure this apparatus is operating fairly and reasonably in its day to day contact with the citizens of our country. In other words, the public expects that its elected representatives will be able to have something to say in a meaningful way about the policies of the government, what they should be and how they are being carried out.
I think it is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that the range and complexity of government today are such that we have reached the point when the members of this house must have their own staff to help them carry out their responsibilities to the Canadian public and the most effective way possible. The responsibilities of the members of this house obviously cover a very wide field, including helping to evolve new policies and legislation and considering the modification of existing policies and legislation to meet changing conditions. All this means, of course, keeping in touch with and being aware of the day to day operations of the departments of government.
Linked up with all this is ensuring that this vast government apparatus deals fairly and reasonably with individual citizens and areas of our country in its contacts with these citizens and areas. This in turn means working to solve the problems faced by individual
June 19, 1967

citizens and areas of this country in their
contacts with the national government and its various departments.
Under today's conditions, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that a member who wants to do all of these things needs to have a staff working directly with him and directly responsible to him. In this way he can keep in touch with government officials, will be able to follow up actively correspondence and requests, and will be given the help he requires in gathering information and carrying out research in order to prepare himself in the most effective way possible for good and meaningful work both in this house and in its committee.
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, when a member is in the house or in a committee he cannot at the same time be talking to officials about particular aspects of policy concerning his riding or the country at large, or be discussing with officials particular problems of concern either to his riding or to the country at large. He certainly cannot be in contact with members of the public or with particular interest groups who wish to express to him personally their views on matters of concern both to them and to the government when at the same time he is obliged to spend time in this house or in committees or in attempting to keep in contact in some way or other with ministers or officials of the government.
A new research branch has been set up in the library of the house and I think it is off to a good start. Generally speaking it has been doing a good job. But no matter how much this branch may be expanded it has by its very nature, certain inherent limitations. For example, in the United States Congress they have evolved a legislative reference service as part of the library of congress which is far beyond anything that we have yet contemplated in this House of Commons with respect to our own research branch. At the same time, even with this extensively developed legislative reference service, members of congress and senators have their own personal staffs of administrative assistants.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
Even with a research branch in parliament, members need help from persons who are directly responsible to them and who can help them focus their attention on particular matters that they wish to deal with either in the house or in the standing committees of the house. Certain work cannot be done effectively by a research branch, such as gathering information through interviewing directly
Provision for Administrative Assistants members of the public or officials of the government. This limitation would also include the gathering of information of a type closely related to the particular political views or policy aims of the member concerned. Also the research branch of the house is not in a position to provide immediate back-up information for members working in the house or in a standing committee who need on the spur of the moment a document or a particular fact to help them put forward in a meaningful way a particular point or argument or to bring out some particular point of view.
I hope it will be possible for this motion to be referred to the special committee on procedure so the details of the scheme contemplated by the motion can be carried out in a way that really is not possible here, not only because the time available for private members' business is limited but because of the particular configuration and approach of the House of Commons itself.
My motion merely attempts to point up the problem and sets out what I consider the necessary way of dealing with it. The details of the scheme, I suggest, can best we worked out by a standing or special committee of the house which could go into all the particular aspects concerned. However, I can say generally that my own view is that it should be left to the individual member himself to decide just exactly what the background and training should be of a potential administrative assistant. Certainly the background of a person who might be hired in this capacity should not be limited to a particular field. There is room for lawyers and people trained in political science, but there is also room for people trained in business management, people from the labour movement and people with backgrounds in economics, sociology and many other fields. Of course the working conditions, pay and so on would have to be sufficiently attractive to retain people of high calibre who would be hired as part of any scheme to provide administrative assistance to members of this house. These would be people who would be willing to make a career in this field, similar to those found in other legislative bodies such as the United States congress.
Of course, another key reason why the member should decide whom he wants to work with him as his assistant is that the member himself knows the kind of individual he wants, one who should share similar policy aims and views in respect of the particular
June 19, 1967
1680	COMMONS
Provision for Administrative Assistants things that should be carried out by parliament and the government.
Again let me say that while the details of the scheme should be left to the committee I think we have reached the stage when it is time for each member to have one or more administrative assistants to assist in various areas. In the initial stages I agree that it may be in order for several members to group together and share an assistant. In this way we could see how the scheme would work out and what further changes might be required. This would certainly increase the real effectiveness of members of this house who would have something more to say about government and be able to influence its direction.
Members of parliament need assistants working directly with and responsible to them. These should be people outside the regular government apparatus to help members keep aware of what is going on and to inform themselves and the public about the details of the operation of the system. We need ways of checking and testing government. These come from knowledge and information.
It has been said that we require improvement and reform of the procedures of this house and that a lot of its work could be done by standing committees. I support this idea very strongly, but a study in committee by members means little if the members themselves are not able to be fully briefed on particular questions beforehand, and of course this calls for the type of proposal included in my notice of motion.
It seems to me that the House of Commons, while certainly a key part of parliament in its broadest sense, is really only a part. Some people still seem to think that all the work of parliament is done in this chamber. That may have been the case at one time but certainy today, with the complexity of government to which I have alluded, the House of Commons as such is useful as a platform from which party leaders and members can speak to the nation and place their views on record, and it is useful for making broad formal decisions. But I suggest it is not really suited for carrying out on a day to day basis the real work of overseeing and directing the operations of modern government. This house may give that appearance, but certainly it is not really suited to carrying out and achieving meaningful legislative oversight.
It is in the public interest for the elected representatives of the Canadian people to


have the facilities to carry out the work expected of them by the people who elect them. Let us not confuse appearance with reality. We may be coming to the stage when we may seem to be giving the appearance of supervising and directing the work of the government, but in reality this is not what we are achieving. Certainly we do not want to reach the stage where we appear to be going through the motions but are not really supervising the workings of government.
The lack of staff obviously limits the degree of supervision possible by members of parliament over the government apparatus. They are sent to exercise a degree of legislative oversight by the Canadian people. The public expects us to perform this task. They are surprised when they find out that we do not have the facilities enabling us to carry out the responsibilities they feel should be carried out in their behalf.
I think I should conclude by using the words I used when I had the opportunity to say something several days ago during the course of the debate on another resolution, which was sent to the standing committee on procedure, in respect of the creation of a system of internes to help train people to know more about our system of government. At that time I said:
Though it may not seem to affect the public as directly as some of the other matters we deal with-economic development and social welfare measures, for example-in the long run it may well turn out to be as important as any of these things if we are to make sure that long after this centennial year is over we shall continue to have a government which is really responsive to the demands and needs of the people of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on this important matter. This debate is an indication that members are thinking about the whole question of greater administrative assistance to them in the discharge of their duties. We had an interesting debate on the resolution of the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Hales) and one sees upcoming on the order paper an equally interesting suggestion by the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. Southam). Indeed, it might have been an efficient discharge of this matter had all three suggestions been referred at the same time because they deal generally with the same subject in similar terms.
I do not think we have to prove to ourselves, nor should we have to state to our public, the complexity of modern legislation. Nor do we have to document the sheer magnitude of the legislative output of modern
June 19, 1967	COMMONS
parliament. Indeed there are some people who think that parliament is becoming too much of a legislative mill, that too much legislation is being processed, and there Eire those observers who sometimes suggest that federal parties are getting into office by making legislative promises which belong in the provincial realm. There is at least reason to look at this contention.
We know too that each and every member is burdened by the compulsive routine of this life. One does not have to be in the House of Commons very long to accumulate a large shelf of documents and legislative outpourings which are not just those of the past but contemporaneous with his own membership in the Chamber. One can think of the statutes only and the lengthy bills, some of which have been over 100 pages.
Everyone knows the difference between legal English and good English in dealing with statutes, and it is not the easiest thing in the world in terms of ready comprehension. We know too of the vast accumulation of committee reports on our shelves. I think in particular of the reports of those committees of which we are not members. A conscientious member wishes to keep somewhat abreast of what is going on in those areas which are not of his own specialization.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
More important, as the mover of the resolution has mentioned, is the need to be prepared as well as possible for the committees of which a member is a part. Sometimes we run into a situation that seems to me to be marring the committee system. Committees dealing with vastly different subject matters are meeting not only on the same day but sometimes at the same hour. Tomorrow morning, for instance, at 9.30 I should have my mind on Viet Nam in one room and be in another room at the same time with my mind on the Prince Edward Island causeway. How I shall bridge that gap, if a pun will be pardoned, I do not really know.
Then, Mr. Speaker, who can say he has read every word of the mountains of royal commission reports which have fallen upon us not in any light way in the last number of years? How many members have read every word of the Carter royal commission report? Has everyone even completed the Gordon royal commission report on economic prospects, or even "Troubled Canada"? Have we all been able to find time to read every single sentence in the 12 volumes of the report on
DEBATES	1681
Provision for Administrative Assistants Atlantic transportation? Other most important studies have been carried out by commissions. I think of the Porter commission and the Bladen commission.
Each of us receives from the Queen's Printer important publications. These are very valuable things. We get every so often a list of books, just a few of the books that come into the parliamentary library, dealing with matters for which in general all parliamentarians have a concern. How many of us manage to read all those books, half of them or even a quarter of them? How can we?
Then there are other documents that come to our desks, reports of various departments and documents from the United Nations, of which the library in parliament is a repository. I suppose we all want to read newspapers. We must read our local newspapers because parliamentary sessions are so long that we are not home nearly as much as we would like to be. We must read the national newspapers so we will know what is going on, what we are doing and what we are supposed to be doing. We should read some international newspapers because the Canadian outlook on the world is not that of many other countries. We all want to or should want to delve into studies by specialists who are neither members of parliament nor civil servants on important matters of public policy.
There is a tremendous range of material that we all want to read and would like to read, but because of the compulsive routine of our job we find it difficult to do so. Therefore it would be most valuable if we had, to put it very simply, at least another pair of eyes and another mind which would assist us in trying to encompass some of the material which would be helpful in the discharge of our duties. This is recognized. I think this resolution deals with one of those subjects which is widely recognized as being important.
We note that in ministerial offices there is a large and continual increase in staff. Ministers have more assistants than ever before. If I could change the spelling of that word I would say that some still need more assistance. But if the executive arm of government which is involved more directly in relationship with the civil service, the bureaucracy, requires assistance, surely those of us who are solely in the legislative arm of government, who must be in a very real sense the watchdogs of the executive as well as the representatives of our people and the custodians of
June 19, 1967
1682	COMMONS DEBATES
Provision for Administrative Assistants public expenditures, cannot but assert ourselves in our desire to be as well equipped as possible in this difficult and complex job into which our people have put us. We want to be as well informed as we can so as to have less reliance upon the officialize of the executive arm, because our legislative function is diminished and diluted if we find ourselves at a loss for technical and detailed information which is available to the executive arm and not to us.
I believe we can better our performance by improving our office function. I do not join with those who maintain that parliament is a hopeless mass of ill informed and poorly motivated people. I do not at all subscribe to that point of view. But I do believe there is a vast area for improvement, and the hon. member's suggestion is one of those which should be followed. I believe that as we increased our information we would increase our effectiveness, and conceivably we could increase our posture of independence within the legislative gamut. I believe that would be all to the good. We realize that now members of the House of Commons are not part time, gentlemanly amateurs in the old British sense. We are certainly not part time when a session lasts 14 months.
