speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleague suggests that we may be amateurs but not gentlemen. I was going to express the hope that surely we are still gentlemen, and considering that we work 14 months in a session we can no longer be called part time amateurs. Considering that it requires a certain degree of stubborn persistence to continue in the job, one discards necessarily some of the amateur aspects. In any case, I believe there is no disgrace in being a professional politician. Indeed I cannot think of any more important role than that of one who devotes his time and energy, and fortune if he has one, to the pursuit of public service.
I was very pleased that such an important body as the Canadian Federation of Agriculture expressed themselves very strongly on this matter. I thought it showed great perception on their part. It showed that they are thinking beyond their own occupational and economic group, that as a responsible organization in the over-all Canadian society they fastened their attention upon the chief political institution in the land and made practical suggestions.

I do not want to cut off anyone else from expressing his views, and I will do something I very rarely do, read something into the record. I quote a comment from a very prominent Canadian. I naturally subscribe to his suggestion. I wish to quote from Professor Paul Fox's volume, "Politics," page 277, the latest edition. He says:
Most M.P.'s have neither the time, the energy, or the money to get any serious research done for themselves.
The result is that they lack fresh and informed thinking to inject into the political process to advance the discussion of issues and to balance the government's strength based on its close relation to the civil service. The same old arguments are bandied back and forth time and time again. The M.P.'s quote the newspapers, and the newspapers quote the M.P.'s, and no one becomes much wiser in the process.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
I do not know that I subscribe totally to the last part of the sentence, although I do admit it is a good sentence. The author continues:
In Congress in the United States, by way of contrast, the facilities for research are plentiful. The Library of Congress has on its staff more than 200 research assistants. Congressmen and Senators may also hire research assistants out of their large expense allowances. The latter amounts vary since they are set by a complicated formula but they average about $50,000 a year per member, in addition to his annual salary of $30,000. Some representatives hire as many as nine personal assistants. Some also have young postgraduate university students working for them as researchers under a plan for "internists" that the American Political Science Association has been running very successfully for more than a decade.
As hon. members know, the "internists" program is a program which has been brought to our attention, and to that of the public, by my colleague, the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Hales).
Many of us have encountered our United States counterparts at international conferences and I think we have all been impressed by the amount of expert assistance which they have. Sometimes we may feel we are extremely well prepared at an international gathering if we have read a couple of books. But then we take our place by some congressman who has perhaps a staff of five or six alert, bright people with him and we realize that there is much to do to improve this matter of administrative assistance in our parliamentary system.
Therefore, I commend the hon. member and I support his resolution most strongly. I commend what has been done so far through the extension of the research facilities of our library. But it is not sufficient and we must
June 19, 1967	COMMONS
follow our agreement on this by more concrete action to improve our function and performance, as the hon. member has suggested.

maintopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support this motion briefly, as well as its principle and purpose. I am glad that we have had this more or less quiet but instructive debate this evening. I want to say to the hon. member who introduced this resolution that I thought he made several very good points in presenting his argument.
I have been in this house for over 22 years and I have seen very great changes during that period because of the developments within government and in our society. The federal government today is becoming more involved with the operations of the provincial governments as a result of agreements with various provincial governments and developments with respect to resources, social welfare measures, and so on. This house has become more involved in the approach of organizations in the country toward legislation. Farmers', labour, business, women's and other organizations make representations to the government and to the various parties in the house with respect to legislation they would like to see adopted. This greater involvement directly with the people has greatly increased the work of parliament and the necessity for specialization with relation to that work.
The hon. member who preceded me paid a tribute to the work being done by the research staff in the library. I endorse what he said. They have been very helpful. I know that I have asked them to prepare several briefs on matters that were of interest to me. However, their work is not extensive enough to meet the requirements of members at the present time. Changes have occurred because of developments in our society which people could not have even foreseen 20 years ago, and therefore the need for these research assistants has arisen largely as the result of hon. members having to deal with complicated legislation and with more legislation than was introduced in the house years ago. They have to read reports of royal commissions. They have to read the reports of special committees or inquiries. They are also supposed to have time to read the reports of international bodies such as the United Nations, the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association, and other organizations. We are presumed to be able to read the reports of the committees of this house. I might say that during the 22 years that I have been here I have never been
DEBATES	1683
Provision jor Administrative Assistants absent from the house on a Saturday or a Sunday more than 12 times because I find it necessary to come here and do what I can to read the reports that are presented to us. We also have to read the annual reports of the various departments.
It is beyond the capacity of the average member to absorb and study such a vast amount of material. That is why I have no hesitation in supporting the principle and purpose of this resolution. Personally, I like to come here on Saturdays and Sundays because the place is quiet and one can sit here without much fear of being disturbed. Other members of the house do the same, particularly those who come from constituencies a long distance from the House of Commons. They also utilize their time in this way. Naturally, members who live in Ontario and Quebec go home on week ends because their constituents expect them there. But even doing the best we can under the circumstances, we are not able to do the research and study of all these reports and problems which I have just mentioned. So, I think it is clearly indicated that members of the house do require research assistants.
This is not a problem which can be dealt with overnight. It requires a great deal of study as to how many research assistants should be provided, the types of persons that should be sought by the various members here representing different political philosophies, and the expenses involved. I am not suggesting for a moment that this house can afford the money that is expended in the Congress of the United States, but I do think we can make a modest start in this direction as the result of a study of the problem. The hon. member who preceded me mentioned the interest of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. Although he hesitated to put on the record the attitude of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, I will do so because I have heard this subject discussed at agricultural meetings as well as at meetings of chambers of commerce and other organizations where the question was asked repeatedly "How in the world do you cope with all the involved questions that come before a member of parliament? Life is becoming more complicated every day." To indicate the interest of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture I will read an article which appeared in the Western Producer of Thursday, June 15, 1967. It reads as follows:
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture is concerned about the growing workload of members of parliament, and would like to see more research

I will begin by dealing with the easiest question, first. The section of the Cumberland railway between Broughton and Louisbourg is excluded because it has no useful value or purpose in the continued operation of the coal mines. Louisbourg was formerly employed as a coal shipping port in winter when Sydney harbour was blocked by ice. It has not been used for such purposes for some years and the coal wharf at Louisburg has been removed. The rail line between Broughton and Louisbourg is in very poor condition seriously limiting train speeds for reasons of safety. If it were to be used, substantial capital would be required to rehabilitate the line. Currently only about one shipment of fish is made over the line each week. The Board of Transport Commissioners held a public hearing in Louisbourg at the end of May to consider an application for abandonment, and reserved judgment.
I have already seen the local press reports of the hearing held by the Transport Board on this matter, and, no doubt, the hon. member has also seen them. I believe he will agree with me that there is no further use for this line in connection with the coal operation, and this is why it is left out.

Mr. Chairman, the remarks made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, not only in the last few minutes but one or two rounds ago, provide the basis for some of the observations that I want to make about the terms of clauses 9 and 10, if I may take them together.
The minister is asking for expropriation powers for certain purposes. When he is asked about the intent that lies behind these expropriation powers he is not able to answer with any precision. I can understand that, because even if he were to know how long a period of time the corporation were prepared to negotiate, and negotiate in vain, before exercising its expropriation powers, he would be unwise to declare any specific time period because this would tend to detract from the genuineness of the negotiation process.
However, Mr. Chairman, more and more people are becoming concerned about the inconsistency with which different departments of this government, as well as the different levels of government in this country, exercise the basic power of expropriation of private property. The Department of National Defence has been known in the past to file plans of expropriation right off the bat without making any pretence whatsoever of negotiation with individual property holders. This was the case with regard to the acquisition of property adjacent to national defence property at Val Cartier, the defence establishment there.
The province of Manitoba has, on previous occasions, filed plans of expropriation without
Cape Breton Development Corporation making any effort to negotiate first with the owners of private property.
I must admit to some confusion about why the government is asking specifically for the power of expropriation in this bill. In any case, we are given to understand by the minister that the exercise of the power of expropriation granted in the bill will be held back until the expiration of a certain period of time, a period of time which is indefinite and which of necessity must remain indefinite as far as we here are concerned. Until such time period has elapsed, the corporation will not exercise this power.
The question then arises, why should one department of the federal government have a certain fixed policy with regard to expropriation practices while another department has a quite different policy? The question begins to arise in many persons' minds that it seems to matter to a considerable extent just who is involved when it comes to governments and crown corporations exercising the power of expropriation. I feel that that observation should be made, and I hope that not only the minister in charge of the bill but all of his colleagues will bear in mind that we need greater consistency in policy on the part of the government.

maintopic: BIRTH CONTROL-INQUIRY AS TO AMENDMENT OF CRIMINAL CODE
BIRTH CONTROL-INQUIRY AS TO AMENDMENT OF CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
On June 9 I asked whether the government would be prepared to give a definite assurance in this house that legislation would be introduced this session to legalize birth control in Canada. I am well aware, as I was when I asked that question, that government spokesmen have made speeches here and there to the effect that birth control will be legalized some time this year. But I would
DEBATES	1705
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion very much like the government to stop playing this cat and mouse game with hon. members and with the public, and let us know definitely here in the house when action is to be taken.
There should be no further need for cat and mouse tactics. Last December, after a long and careful study, the standing committee on health and welfare recommended that birth control be made legal, that it should no longer be an offence under the Criminal Code. The Committee recommended also that regulations: should be introduced under the Food and Drugs Act concerning the distribution and advertising of contraceptives and that henceforth in Canada birth control should be left to the individual conscience.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
In other words, individuals who believed in getting information and birth control devices should have the right to do so without it being considered a crime. Those people who, because of religion or conscience or anything of that type, did not believe in such things should not have any information or devices forced upon them. It is very significant, Mr. Speaker, that throughout the long sessions of the health and welfare committee only one organization, a smaller church body, wanted to keep the Criminal Code the way it is.
It is not my purpose at the moment to debate the pros and cons of birth control. That has already been done. My purpose is to ask assurance that legislation to give effect to our committee recommendation, and to legalize birth control, will be brought in this session. I want the assurance of the government to that effect, and I want it for two or three reasons.
I think it is very important that we lose no time in getting rid of a bad law. We were assured by delegation after delegation from different bodies who appeared before the committee that this is a bad law on the statute books, a law which cannot be enforced. It is a poor thing to keep a law of this type on the statute books because it breeds disrespect and disrepute for the law.
The Canadian Catholic Conference of Bishops was one of the bodies which strongly urged that the legislation in its present form be removed from the Criminal Code.
In the second place, I would very much like to see us without fear in this centennial year move Canada at least into the twentieth century, along with a lot of other countries, in this matter of the legalization of birth control. On June 9, when I raised this question, I mentioned that France had been the most
1706	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion recent country to announce it was moving forward to legalize birth control. France is worried about a falling birth rate.
Our own birth rate in Canada has been falling somewhat, although I do not believe to such a degree that it is worrying anybody. However, in France they are concerned about it but they are not hoping to maintain the birth rate by keeping birth control illegal. They are taking a much wiser course. They are beginning to think that by encouraging subsidized housing for married couples and by other measures they can increase the birth rate to the level which they want.
I think it is high time in this country that we wiped out the hypocritical attitude we have had toward birth control. It is a peculiar thing when you find a great big municipality like Scarborough has been put in the position of illegally operating a birth control clinic for some time now, and that every minister, every priest and every physician who made birth control information available with respect to the handling of contraceptives has been guilty of an illegal act. I, for one, would like to make sure that the government without fail is going to introduce legislation of this type this session, and will announce so here in this house which is the proper place.
I see no reason why the minister should get up and say it is going to be announced in due course. Everybody outside has been told it is coming in this session. I would like to ask the minister, please make this announcement in the house so that we will know once and for all, and so that the Canadian people will realize this thing is going to be introduced as definite legislation this year.

He said that it was bizarre that Canada lacks a single Japanese speaking trade commissioner.

Japanese. In other words, that the department would have to start from scratch now.
More than one university in Canada conducts courses in the Japanese language. The University of British Columbia has been offering courses in the Japanese language since 1956. This I know because I was a member of the first class to study Japanese at the University of British Columbia. There were 14 in that class, and classes have been held since then. Admittedly not everyone in the class would be fluent in the language, but they would at least have a groundwork.
If the department conducted a recruiting campaign in places such as universities or among the Japanese-Canadian community, it might not be at all necessary to initiate a special language course. But even if this were the case, Mr. Speaker, we would not have to start from scratch; we would be able to find applicants who would at least have the basics of the language.
We in British Columbia and in the west of Canada are extremely concerned, and have been for a long time, about the whole question of trade promotion and trade commissioners in the Pacific rim. We welcomed the announcement of the Prime Minister the other day that very shortly an ambassador to Korea would be appointed. This is something to which we have looked forward for a long time. We in British Columbia hope that many of the departments of the federal government will live up to the statement that is often made by various representatives of the government, namely that the federal government is vitally concerned in the Pacific rim.

Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin (Acting Minister of
Trade and Commerce): Mr. Speaker, the suggested answer by the Department of Trade and Commerce repeats the argument that linguists consider a two year training period to be minimal in achieving a reasonable degree of fluency in this very difficult language. Departmental assignments abroad are rotational and it has been the view that a two year training period is too costly in terms of its proportion of an officer's career to be realistic when the posting time in Japan is two and a half years. Of course, entrance to the department is open to Canadians of Japanese origin and Canadians who speak Japanese, so I would think that those who felt they would like to take up this work would have a very good chance of being accepted.
The department does, of course, have local nationals on strength to translate and interpret, and it employs two commercial officers in its Tokyo office who are fluent in Japanese. These are in addition to its clerical and stenographic staff. Because of the high proportion of Japanese businessmen who are fluent in the English language, the department has encountered no real difficulty in conducting its business in Japan.
Personally I think the suggestion made by the hon. member that a special contest or drive should take place is a good one, and I will pass it on personally to the minister of the Department of Trade and Commerce.
